newsitem.title: ITALY: Castro slams killer capitalism at food summit.
newsitem.headline: Castro slams killer capitalism at food summit.

text.p: Cuban President Fidel Castro, describing hunger as daily genocide, told a U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit on Saturday that the Cold War was over but capitalism and consumerism were killing millions.
"Capitalism, neoliberalism, the laws of a wild market, the external debt, underdevelopment and the unequal terms of reference" were killing people, Castro said.
"Hunger, the inseparable companion of the poor, is the offspring of the unequal distribution of the wealth and the injustices in this world," Castro said.
"The rich do not know hunger."

His words found a less forceful echo among some other developing countries, with Bangladesh asking the world's powers what they were waiting for now that the days of East-West conflict and the arms race were long gone.
Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, one of the few speakers from developed nations in the morning session, said free trade and international cooperation were required.
He said the developed countries carried a particular responsibility for the less well off. "We cannot ignore an estimated billion people living in abject poverty," he said.
"International solidarity is crucial."

Castro, the West's longest surviving Cold War antagonist, delivered his long-awaited speech to loud applause from developing nations as he slammed the rich world and criticised the summit's aims to halve the number of hungry in the world within 20 years as shamefully modest.

"If the world is rightly moved by accidents and natural or social catastrophes that bring death to hundreds or thousands of people, why is it not equally moved by that genocide which is taking place every day in front of our eyes?

He blasted military spending and arms sales to developing states, asking "why are increasingly sophisticated weapons still being produced after the Cold War is over? What are those weapons for if not to dominate the world?"

Sheikh Hasina, prime minister of Bangladesh, whose country was at the centre of a crisis at the last food summit in 1974, told the assembled delegates that "the threat of conflict between East and West is well behind us".

And she said the hungry were asking one question: "What are we all and the world powers waiting for to use the huge resources swallowed up by our budgets for human destruction to engage in outright battle with poverty and hunger?"
"The hungry cannot wait," she said.
"Never has the sheer number of men, women and children suffering from hunger been so high.
"Never have so many people, uprooted by natural disasters and human cruelty alike, crowded along roads and straggled their way on to makeshift hovels or pitifully flimsy vessels."

The five-day Food Summit, which ends on Sunday, has been dominated by debate about the crisis in Central Africa, where hundreds of thousands of starving Rwandan and Burundian refugees have begun a slow trek back to their homes.
Delegates have called repeatedly for actions to prevent such scenes happening again and to avert widespread civil unrest in countries in the region.
The problems were highlighted when soldiers in the Central African Republic were reported to have launched a mutiny after forcibly taking weapons from an armoury.

The country's president, Ange-Felix Patasse, denied that a mutiny was under way and said common criminals who had escaped were trying to spread panic. "Nothing abnormal," was his response when asked by Reuters at the summit.

Castro's rare trip to Europe has been widely expected to involve an historic meeting with Pope John Paul, and the Vatican's foreign minister said he planned to discuss the subject with the leader at the summit on Saturday.
A meeting between Castro and the Pope would cement improving relations between Cuba and the Roman Catholic Church and could pave the way for the Pontiff to visit Cuba next year.
